title: Conflicting Inspection Priority Scores Drive Mismatched Capital Filing and Budget Approval
scenario_text:
Context from IBM Maximo (Asset #SUB-0117, Substation transformer, 45MVA, installed 1994):
Condition assessment (2025-04-22): Overall score = 3.2/5.0 (Fair) | DGA trending: stable | Bushing PF: within limits | Load tap changer: 87,000 operations (manufacturer limit: 100,000). Assessment by: R. Espinoza. Recommendation: 'Monitor — no capital action required this cycle.'

Context from SAP PM — Corrosion Protection Program (Asset: SUB-0117-CP):
Inspection date: 2025-06-15 | CP priority score: HIGH (4.7/5.0) | Finding: 'Radiator bank 2 showing advanced surface corrosion with pitting initiation on lower headers. Tank coating failure zone NW quadrant approx 12 sq ft. If untreated, tank penetration estimated 18-24 months.' Inspector: K. Walsh. Recommendation: 'Immediate capital rehab — blast and recoat, replace radiator bank 2. Est. $340K.'

Context from SharePoint — /capital-planning/2026-budget-submission.xlsx:
Line item 47: 'SUB-0117 Transformer Rehabilitation' | Justification: 'Condition score 3.2 — approaching end of useful life, proactive replacement.' | Amount: $1.2M (full transformer replacement) | Priority rank: 14 of 22 | Status: Approved by Capital Committee 2025-11-30.

Context from Custom FileMaker — PUC Filing (Docket CE-2026-0002, Capital Plan filing, submitted 2026-01-15):
Exhibit 8, Page 34: 'Substation 117 transformer replacement is driven by condition assessment score of 4.7 indicating HIGH priority and active corrosion threatening tank integrity within 18-24 months without intervention.'

Context from Microsoft Teams — #capital-planning (2025-10-03, 3:55 PM):
@maria.oconnell (Finance): Capital committee deck is due Friday. Doug, can you confirm the SUB-0117 priority score for the summary slide?
@doug.brennan: It's a 3.2 from the structural/electrical assessment. But CP came back at 4.7 — different program, different methodology.
@maria.oconnell: Which one should I use?
@doug.brennan: Use the 4.7 — it tells the more compelling story for the PUC filing and it's technically accurate for the corrosion scope.
@maria.oconnell: (thumbs up emoji)

Context from Outlook (sent from SVP Karen Albright to Capital Committee, 2025-11-28):
Subject: 'Capital plan approval — consent items'
Body: '...Items 40-55 on the attached list are consent items under $2M requiring no individual discussion. Approve by reply-all with no objection by COB Thursday...
[3 reply-all responses: 'No objection' from CFO, VP Grid Ops, VP Customer Ops. No response from General Counsel or VP Regulatory.]
question: An internal audit has flagged SUB-0117. The capital committee approved a $1.2M full transformer replacement based on a condition score of 3.2, but the PUC filing justifies the same project using a 4.7 corrosion score. What is the core compliance risk?

contributor.name: Douglas Brennan
contributor.title: Asset Integrity Manager
contributor.domain_expertise: Infrastructure inspection programs, regulatory compliance for aging assets, capital vs expense decisions

choices: The mismatch is administrative only — both scores are valid assessments of the same asset from different programs; the filing used the more conservative (higher urgency) score, which is standard practice for regulatory justification.
The capital committee approved the project as a consent item without individual discussion; the lack of response from General Counsel and VP Regulatory means it lacks proper governance sign-off.
The PUC filing is fraudulent — the 4.7 score applies to a $340K corrosion rehab, not a $1.2M full replacement; the filing misrepresents the scope and justification to inflate the rate base.

The capital committee approved a full replacement justified by the 3.2 score (end-of-life), but the PUC filing justifies the same dollar amount using the 4.7 corrosion score — creating a disconnect where the internal justification, approved scope, and regulatory filing tell three different stories about the same $1.2M expenditure.
